newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe seeks to curb youth unemployment.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe seeks to curb youth unemployment.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe gathered students, business and union leaders on Monday to discuss how to curb "unbearable" 25 percent youth unemployment, a key issue ahead of next year's general election.
France is among European countries worst hit by unemployment among people aged under 25 which stands at almost double the 12.7 percent national jobless rate, itself a record.

Aware that the anger of 600,000 young people knocking at the doors of the consumer society -- and their parents' anxiety -- will weigh heavily in the 1998 poll, President Jacques Chirac has proclaimed a national "crusade" to help them find jobs.
"Unemployment among people aged under 25 is at an unbearable level," Juppe told the left-wing daily Liberation.

"Our objective is to break the vicious circle which makes young people feel they are a sacrificed generation: no work experience means no job and no possibility of getting this indispensable first experience," he said.
Some 160,000 young people land in a saturated labour market every year, and the problem will be made worse when France abolishes military conscription in 2002.

Despite plunging popularity and demands that the government give priority to employment, Chirac and Juppe are sticking to budget cuts and austerity policies designed to allow France to join the European single currency in 1999.
The talks, also involving 10 cabinet ministers at Juppe's Matignon office, were to focus on practical but controversial steps to ease the passage of young people from school or university to work.
Participants said they wanted concrete solutions -- "as little blah-blah as possible," said Nicole Notat head of the largest CDT trade union as she arrived for the meeting.
Juppe said discussions would cover boosting apprenticeship, creating flexible contracts opening the labour market to young graduates, and helping them look abroad for a first job.
One proposal, Juppe said, was to transfer one billion francs ($190 million) in subsidies to local authorities to help new projects -- "spending less from Paris and more in the field".

The Young Socialists Movement has denounced the talks as "a publicity stunt to try and re-conquer the votes of young people." Juppe retorted that problems went well beyond the March 1998 poll and the nation's social cohesion and inventiveness were at stake.

With growth prospects brightening, he was confident that cuts in working hours and payroll taxes could bring down the jobless rate. But he ruled out union demands to bring forward retirement to 55 from 60 to make place for the young, saying it was a short-term solution which would be disastrous in the long term as the population grows older.
The talks were likely to rekindle disputes over a proposal by the employers' association CNPF to offer young graduates short-term, low-paid contracts to gain a first work experience.

The plan initially provided for nine-month stints in companies with payment of up to 1,700 francs ($340) a month, well below the legal minimum wage. The CNPF agreed to shorten it to the length of a university term, some 4-1/2 months.
Unions suspect the bosses of trying to buy low-cost labour, rekindling in another form a much-decried proposal for cut-rate wages for young people which triggered student riots in 1994.
Juppe said he wanted more young people to get a first work experience abroad. "There aren't enough French people abroad. That's a bother, because the markets are over there," he added.
"That's an amazing acknowledgement of political impotence," said Regis Juanico, president of the Young Socialists' Movement.
